Complete native R discrete Frechet and dynamic time warping contracts

etr_native_distance_contracts.Rd

Independent Python-free implementations of the public eyetrajectoriespy 1.2.0 methods discrete_frechet_distance, dynamic_time_warping_distance and pairwise_dynamic_time_warping_distances. They expose explicit ordered coupling paths, two DTW step patterns, optional Sakoe-Chiba constraints and deterministic cost audits. Python is only used by optional external reference tests.

Usage

etr_discrete_frechet(a, b, dimension_weights = NULL,
                      return_coupling = FALSE,
                      python_boundary_mode = FALSE)
etr_dynamic_time_warping(a, b, dimension_weights = NULL,
                          window_radius = NULL,
                          step_pattern = "symmetric1",
                          normalize = FALSE,
                          return_path = FALSE,
                          python_boundary_mode = FALSE)
etr_pairwise_dtw_full(x, dimensions = NULL, dimension_weights = NULL,
                      window_radius = NULL,
                      step_pattern = "symmetric1", normalize = FALSE,
                      python_boundary_mode = FALSE)

Arguments

a,b

Complete numeric point-by-dimension matrices. Both require at least one time-ordered point and the same number of channels. In python_boundary_mode=TRUE, finite numeric-looking character or logical matrices and regular nested scalar point rows are also accepted.

dimension_weights

NULL or one finite nonnegative numeric weight per channel. At least one weight must be strictly positive. In source-boundary mode, numeric-compatible character or logical weights are also accepted.

return_coupling

Logical: if TRUE return a detailed optimal discrete Frechet coupling and local distances; otherwise a numeric scalar.

window_radius

NULL or a nonnegative integer Sakoe-Chiba window in sample-index units. It must permit connection between the endpoints.

step_pattern

DTW recursion "symmetric1" (all selected moves weight one) or "symmetric2" (diagonal moves weight two, horizontal/vertical moves weight one).

normalize

Logical. Only supported with "symmetric2". If TRUE, return raw cumulative distance divided by n_a+n_b.

return_path

Logical. If TRUE, return the full audited alignment path, local distances, weighted distances, counts and provenance.

python_boundary_mode

Logical. Explicitly opt in to bounded Python 1.2 np.asarray(..., dtype=float) point and weight conversion. Defaults to FALSE, preserving strict native R input validation. For pairwise DTW, TRUE allows NumPy-compatible finite dimension weights; the trajectory values must still be a native complete trajectory set.

x

Complete native etr_trajectory_set.

dimensions

NULL to use all stored channels, or distinct ordered channel names selecting the comparison dimensions.

Value

etr_discrete_frechet() returns a scalar or an etr_discrete_frechet_result list with distance, coupling, local_distances, n_points_a, n_points_b, n_dimensions and provenance. coupling is an integer two-column matrix with **zero-based** pair indices matching the Python result.

etr_dynamic_time_warping() returns a scalar or an etr_dtw_result list with distance, zero-based integer path, local_distances, step_weights, weighted_local_costs, raw_distance, optional normalized_distance, path_length, mean_local_distance, dimension counts, window_radius, step_pattern, optional normalization_denominator and provenance. Python's None fields are R NULL.

etr_pairwise_dtw_full() returns a symmetric numeric matrix without dimension labels; the diagonal is zero.

Details

All algorithms are discrete, not continuous, and never use recorded time, interpolate missing samples or change spatial coordinate units. They use weighted Euclidean local costs, retain monotonicity of the coupled trajectory sample indices, and resolve exactly tied predecessors in the upstream order: diagonal, then advancing the first trajectory, then advancing the second.

The upstream Python dynamic_time_warping_distance implements symmetric1 as raw path-visit costs, not normalized by path length. The normalizable symmetric2 recursion uses diagonal costs twice; when requested, normalization divides raw cumulative cost by the sequence length sum, not the number of alignment-path nodes.

With python_boundary_mode=TRUE, the native R implementation also performs finite numeric-string and Boolean input conversion before computing the distance. This is a source-backed *subset* of NumPy's coercion domain; it does not assert acceptance of arbitrary Python objects, scientific equivalence for all floating-point overflow boundaries, or identity of Python dataclasses versus native R S3 result records.

The native R implementation imposes an explicit resource guard: at most 5e6 point pairs for dense dynamic programming. The published Python 1.2 function has no equivalent fixed limit. The complete native R parity register consequently remains unqualified for full behavioral equivalence, even after fixed numerical test cases succeed. The R results reproduce documented Python provenance fields as ordinary R named lists but have not been qualified for Python serialization/JSON round-trip equivalence.

The older etr_frechet(), etr_dtw() and etr_pairwise_dtw() remain available unchanged for existing R users. The new functions express additional Python 1.2 behavior.

Examples

a <- matrix(c(0, 1, 2), ncol = 1)
b <- matrix(c(.1, 1.1, 2.1), ncol = 1)
f <- etr_discrete_frechet(a, b, return_coupling = TRUE)
d <- etr_dynamic_time_warping(a, b, return_path = TRUE)
n <- etr_dynamic_time_warping(a, b, step_pattern = "symmetric2",
                               normalize = TRUE, window_radius = 0L)
